newsitem.title: USA: Inoculation program set for U.S. schoolchildren.
newsitem.headline: Inoculation program set for U.S. schoolchildren.

text.p: Thousands of U.S. schoolchildren exposed to tainted strawberries were to begin lining up for hepatitis inoculations on Thursday as federal officials tried to determine how the berries were infected.

Some 153 children and teachers in several Michigan schools were diagnosed with the disease, and students and school staff in a half-dozen other states may have been exposed to frozen strawberries carrying the virus, U.S. officials said.
A San Diego fruit processor, Andrews & Williamson, could face criminal charges if authorities confirm the bad strawberries came from Mexico, as suspected by U.S. Agriculture Department officials.
Companies must certify in writing that the products they sell to the goverment school lunch programs are grown in the United States.
The president of A&W resigned hours after news reports of the disease outbreak sent panic waves through schools in 16 states.

"At this point, no cases of Hepatitis A associated with these strawberries outside the state of Michigan have been identified," said Dr. David Satcher, director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. "Consumers outside this limited setting should not be concerned."

But some 9,000 schoolchildren in California and 2,000 in Georgia were preparing to receive inoculations of immune globulin on Thursday. The medicine is not a vaccine, but contains antibodies to help prevent kids from getting the illness.
Michigan state health officials said they had already begun inoculations for children who might have been exposed.

The disease and its flu-like symptoms typically makes people feel sick for two to eight weeks but is rarely fatal. Hepatitis A, which is common in developing countries, is spread by poor personal hygiene or when food or water is contaminated by sewage.

Officials said 28 Michigan counties received the frozen strawberries, which were shipped to the state last December. The berries were processed and packed by the California company last April and May.
Michigan officials said health agencies throughout the state had given thousands of injections to schoolchildren.

Public health officials in Los Angeles planned to begin administering inoculations on Thursday to students and school workers at 18 elementary, middle and high schools who may have been exposed to the virus. Officials said they would start with those who ate the tainted fruit mixture, and expand the shots as more supplies of the drug become available.

While an estimated 9,000 Los Angeles students and staff may have been exposed to the tainted fruit, officials said the number of people who actually ate the fruit and need immune globulin shots will be substantially less than that.

Ruben Zacarias, deputy superintendent for the Los Angeles Unifed School District, said schools handed out parental consent forms written in five languages to explain what happened and why it was necessary to receive shots.
Officials stressed there was little risk of serious health problems if students and staff were treated quickly. The disease has an incubation period of 14 days.
A&W shipped strawberries to 17 states, but only six received berries from the tainted batch, USDA officials said.
Chicago school officials said that virtually all of the 1,320 cases of strawberries were still in warehouses, and there were no known cases of hepatitis among local students.
In Georgia, hepatitis inoculations were set to begin for nearly 2,000 students believed to have been exposed to the virus through school lunches.
No tainted lots landed in Florida, but state officials urged 19 school districts and a small number of prisons that received strawberries to pull the food off the shelves.

Iowa said state schools received one batch of possibly tainted berries that may have been served in some schools as late as last week, but so far there were no reports of students suffering Hepatitis A symptoms.

Investigators from the Agriculture Department, the Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control searched the packing records of the California processor, trying to track down where all the berries went.
The suspect berries were contaminated either in the field where harvested or at the processing plant, FDA officials said.
"Where the source of introduction of the virus was, we're not sure," said Dr. Michael Friedman, deputy commissioner of the FDA. "We're in the process of trying to identify that right now."
